blocks.html: By far, the most utilized loop statement in C++ is the for-statement. The for statement (also called a for loop) is preferred when we have an obvious loop variable because it lets us easily and concisely define, initialize, test, and change the value of loop variables.

The easiest way to initially understand how a for-statement works is to convert it into an equivalent while-statement:

blocks.title: Evaluation of for-statements
blocks.html: Evaluation of for-statements
A for-statement is evaluated in 3 parts:
blocks.preview: A for-statement is evaluated in 3 parts:

blocks.html: First, the init-statement is executed. This only happens once when the loop is initiated. The init-statement is typically used for variable definition and initialization. These variables have “loop scope”, which really just is a form of block scope where these variables exist from the point of definition through the end of the loop statement. In our while-loop equivalent, you can see that the init-statement is inside a block that contains the loop, so the variables defined in the init-statement go out of scope when the block containing the loop ends.
blocks.preview: First, the init-statement is executed. This only happens once when the loop is i

blocks.html: Second, with each loop iteration, the condition is evaluated. If this evaluates to true, the statement is executed. If this evaluates to false, the loop terminates and execution continues with the next statement beyond the loop.
blocks.preview: Second, with each loop iteration, the condition is evaluated. If this evaluates

blocks.html: Finally, after the statement is executed, the end-expression is evaluated. Typically, this expression is used to increment or decrement the loop variables defined in the init-statement. After the end-expression has been evaluated, execution returns to the second step (and the condition is evaluated again).
blocks.preview: Finally, after the statement is executed, the end-expression is evaluated. Typic

blocks.html:
Key insight

The order of execution for the different parts of a for-statement is as follows:

  • Init-statement
  • Condition (if this is false, the loop terminates here).
  • Loop body
  • End-expression (then jumps back to condition)

Note that the end-expression executes after the loop statement, and then the condition is re-evaluated.

This helps reduce errors.

blocks.title: More for-loop examples
blocks.html: More for-loop examples
Here’s an example of a function that uses a for-loop to calculate integer exponents:
blocks.preview: Here’s an example of a function that uses a for-loop to calculate integer expone

#include <cstdint> // for fixed-width integers

// returns the value base ^ exponent -- watch out for overflow!
std::int64_t pow(int base, int exponent)
{
    std::int64_t total{ 1 };

    for (int i{ 0 }; i < exponent; ++i)
        total *= base;

    return total;
}
This function returns the value base^exponent (base to the exponent power).
blocks.preview: This function returns the value base^exponent (base to the exponent power).

blocks.html: This is a straightforward incrementing for-loop, with i looping from 0 up to (but excluding) exponent.

In all cases, total is initialized to 1.
If exponent is 0, the for-loop will execute 0 times. total (with value 1) is returned, which is equivalent to base^0.
If exponent is 1, the for-loop will execute 1 time. total (with value 1) is multiplied by base, so it is now has value base, which is equivalent to base^1, which is then returned.
If exponent is 2, the for-loop will execute 2 times. total (with value 1) is multiplied by base twice, so it now has value base * base, which is equivalent to base^2, which is then returned.

blocks.title: The perils of operator!= in for-loop conditions
blocks.html: The perils of operator!= in for-loop conditions
When writing a loop condition involving a value, we can often write the condition in many different ways. The following two loops execute identically:
blocks.preview: When writing a loop condition involving a value, we can often write the conditio

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    for (int i { 0 }; i < 10; ++i) // uses <
         std::cout << i;

    for (int i { 0 }; i != 10; ++i) // uses !=
         std::cout << i;

     return 0;
}
So which should we prefer? The former is the better choice, as it will terminate even if i jumps over the value 10, whereas the latter will not. The following example demonstrates this:
blocks.preview: So which should we prefer? The former is the better choice, as it will terminate

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    for (int i { 0 }; i < 10; ++i) // uses <, still terminates
    {
         std::cout << i;
         if (i == 9) ++i; // jump over value 10
    }

    for (int i { 0 }; i != 10; ++i) // uses !=, infinite loop
    {
         std::cout << i;
         if (i == 9) ++i; // jump over value 10
    }

     return 0;
}

Best practice

Avoid operator!= when doing numeric comparisons in the for-loop condition. Prefer operator< or operator<= where possible.

blocks.title: Off-by-one errors
blocks.html: Off-by-one errors

One of the biggest problems that new programmers have with for-loops (and other loops that utilize counters) are off-by-one errors. Off-by-one errors occur when the loop iterates one too many or one too few times to produce the desired result.

blocks.html: Here’s an example:
blocks.preview: Here’s an example:

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    // oops, we used operator< instead of operator<=
    for (int i{ 1 }; i < 5; ++i)
    {
        std::cout << i << ' ';
    }

    std::cout << '\n';

    return 0;
}
This program is supposed to print 1 2 3 4 5, but it only prints 1 2 3 4 because we used the wrong relational operator.

blocks.html: Omitted expressions

It is possible to write for loops that omit any or all of the statements or expressions. For example, in the following example, we’ll omit the init-statement and end-expression, leaving only the condition:

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int i{ 0 };
    for ( ; i < 10; ) // no init-statement or end-expression
    {
        std::cout << i << ' ';
        ++i;
    }

    std::cout << '\n';

    return 0;
}

We have done so purely for academic purposes in this example, but there are cases where not defining a loop variable (because you already have one) or not incrementing it in the end-expression (because you’re incrementing it some other way) is desired.

blocks.title: For-loops with multiple counters
blocks.html: For-loops with multiple counters

Although for-loops typically iterate over only one variable, sometimes for-loops need to work with multiple variables. To assist with this, the programmer can define multiple variables in the init-statement, and can make use of the comma operator to change the value of multiple variables in the end-expression:
blocks.preview: Although for-loops typically iterate over only one variable, sometimes for-loops

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    for (int x{ 0 }, y{ 9 }; x < 10; ++x, --y)
        std::cout << x << ' ' << y << '\n';

    return 0;
}
This loop defines and initializes two new variables: x and y. It iterates x over the range 0 to 9, and after each iteration x is incremented and y is decremented.

blocks.title: Nested for-loops
blocks.html: Nested for-loops
Like other types of loops, for-loops can be nested inside other loops. In the following example, we’re nesting a for-loop inside another for-loop:
blocks.preview: Like other types of loops, for-loops can be nested inside other loops. In the fo

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
	for (char c{ 'a' }; c <= 'e'; ++c) // outer loop on letters
	{
		std::cout << c; // print our letter first
		
		for (int i{ 0 }; i < 3; ++i) // inner loop on all numbers
			std::cout << i;

		std::cout << '\n';
	}

	return 0;
}
For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs in its entirety. Consequently, the output is:
blocks.preview: For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs in its entirety. Conse

blocks.html: Here’s some more detail on what’s happening here. The outer loop runs first, and char c is initialized to 'a'. Then c <= 'e' is evaluated, which is true, so the loop body executes. Since c is set to 'a', this first prints a. Next the inner loop executes entirely (which prints 0, 1, and 2). Then a newline is printed. Now the outer loop body is finished, so the outer loop returns to the top, c is incremented to 'b', and the loop condition is re-evaluated. Since the loop condition is still true the next iteration of the outer loop begins. This prints b012\n. And so on.

blocks.title: Variables used only inside a loop should be defined inside the loop
blocks.html: Variables used only inside a loop should be defined inside the loop

New programmers often think that creating variables is expensive, so that it is better to create a variable once (and then assign values to it) than create it many times (and use initialization). That leads to loops that look like some variation of the following:
blocks.preview: New programmers often think that creating variables is expensive, so that it is

blocks.html:
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int i {}; // i defined outside loop
    for (i = 0; i < 10; ++i) // i assigned value
    {
        std::cout << i << ' ';        
    }

    // i can still be accessed here

    std::cout << '\n';

    return 0;
}

However, creating a variable has no cost -- it is the initialization that has a cost, and there is typically no cost difference between initialization and assignment. The above example makes i available beyond the loop. Unless using a variable beyond the loop is required, defining a variable outside the loop is likely to have two consequences:
blocks.preview: However, creating a variable has no cost -- it is the initialization that has a

blocks.html:
1. It makes our program more complex, as we have to read more code to see where the variable is used.
  2. It may actually be slower because the compiler may not be able to optimize a variable with a larger scope as effectively.
blocks.preview: It makes our program more complex, as we have to read more code to see where the

blocks.html: Consistent with our best practice to define variables in the smallest reasonable scope possible, a variable that is only used within a loop should be defined inside the loop rather than outside.
blocks.preview: Consistent with our best practice to define variables in the smallest reasonable

blocks.html:
Best practice

Variables used only inside a loop should be defined inside the scope of the loop.
blocks.preview: Best practiceVariables used only inside a loop should be defined inside the scope of the loop.

blocks.title: Conclusion
blocks.html: Conclusion

For-statements are the most commonly used loop in the C++ language because they place all of the necessary information about loop variables, loop condition, and loop variable modifies at the top of the loops, which helps reduce errors. Even though its syntax is typically a bit confusing to new programmers, you will see for-loops so often that you will understand them in no time at all!

blocks.questionHtml: Write a function named sumTo() that takes an integer parameter named value, and returns the sum of all the numbers from 1 to value.
blocks.solutionHtml:
int sumTo(int value)
{
    int total{ 0 };
    for (int i{ 1 }; i <= value; ++i)
        total += i;

    return total;
}

blocks.questionHtml: What’s wrong with the following for loop?
blocks.solutionHtml: This for-loop executes as long as i >= 0. In other words, it runs until i is negative. However, because i is unsigned, i can never go negative. Consequently, this loop will run for-ever (ha ha)! Generally, it’s a good idea to avoid looping on unsigned variables unless necessary.

blocks.html:
// Print all numbers from 9 to 0
for (unsigned int i{ 9 }; i >= 0; --i)
    std::cout << i<< ' ';

blocks.questionHtml: Fizz Buzz is a simple math game used to teach children about divisibility. It is also sometimes used as an interview question to assess basic programming skills.
blocks.solutionHtml:
// h/t to reader Waldo for suggesting this quiz
#include <iostream>

void fizzbuzz(int count)
{
	for (int i{ 1 }; i <= count; ++i)
	{
		if (i % 3 == 0 && i % 5 == 0)
		{
			std::cout << "fizzbuzz\n";
		}
		else if (i % 3 == 0)
		{
			std::cout << "fizz\n";
		}
		else if (i % 5 == 0)
		{
			std::cout << "buzz\n";
		}
		else
		{
			std::cout << i << '\n';
		}
	} // end for loop
}

int main()
{
	fizzbuzz(15);

	return 0;
}

blocks.html: The rules of the game are simple: Starting at 1, and counting upward, replace any number divisible only by three with the word “fizz”, any number only divisible by five with the word “buzz”, and any number divisible by both 3 and 5 with the word “fizzbuzz”.

blocks.questionHtml: Modify the FizzBuzz program you wrote in the previous quiz to add the rule that numbers divisible by seven should be replaced with “pop”. Run the program for 150 iterations.
blocks.hintHtml: Hint: Use a boolean variable to keep track of whether a number has matched one of the conditions.
blocks.solutionHtml:
// h/t to reader Waldo for suggesting this quiz
#include <iostream>

void fizzbuzz(int count)
{
	for (int i{ 1 }; i <= count; ++i)
	{
		bool printed{ false };
		if (i % 3 == 0)
		{
			std::cout << "fizz";
			printed = true;
		}
		if (i % 5 == 0)
		{
			std::cout << "buzz";
			printed = true;
		}
		if (i % 7 == 0)
		{
			std::cout << "pop";
			printed = true;
		}

		if (!printed)
			std::cout << i;

		std::cout << '\n';
	} // end for loop
}

int main()
{
	fizzbuzz(150);

	return 0;
}
